name: FixGrid

gate1.read: Any FixGrid customer, on any plan, can turn on the API themselves today. A company admin creates the key inside FixGrid. There is no extra fee, no API add-on, and no sales call.

gate2.read: You can open, assign, complete, cancel, and reopen work orders from your own tools. Webhooks tell you about new tickets, status changes, and assignments. The published documentation shows no way to schedule appointments, upload photos, read back notes, add or edit vendors, or handle estimates, invoices, or owner approvals through the API. Coverage of 70.45% is below the 85% an A needs, so gate 2 holds the letter at B.

mcp.note: No official MCP server was found (zero MCP Registry results and no /mcp page on either domain), so the MCP step did not apply.

reads.c2: The API behaves predictably. Errors come back with clear codes, retries are safe, paging is reliable, changes can be synced, webhooks are signed, and two people can't silently overwrite the same ticket. The weak spots are short notice for breaking changes (90 days, and one change already skipped it), no live warning as you approach the rate limit, and cost figures sent as plain decimal numbers.
reads.c3: You can give each tool or AI agent its own key, limit it to reading or to just the actions it needs, and revoke it yourself. The published documentation shows no API sandbox, so testing happens against a real account. There is also no "sign in with FixGrid" option, so connecting a third-party tool means handing it a key.
reads.c4: A developer or an AI coding tool can build from the public spec and the one-file text docs without logging in. The reference shows sample requests but not sample responses. A builder leans on the field tables to know what comes back.

checklist.note: List, fetch, create, update, reopen, and add a note.
Change status, reopen a closed ticket, filter by status, and get a webhook on each change.
Set or clear the assigned technician or vendor, look up staff, and get an assignment webhook.
Read-only. The published documentation shows no way to create, update, or deactivate a vendor.
The published documentation shows no appointment, scheduled date, or time window on work orders.
A move-in can record the residents, but the published documentation shows no way to read resident records.
Readable with filters and change syncing, plus notice and move-in writes. The property roster comes from your PMS.

checklist.item: Photos or attachments on a work order
checklist.note: One photo link is readable. The published documentation shows no photo upload.

checklist.item: Messages or comments on a work order
checklist.note: You can add a note, but notes cannot be read back through the API yet.
A PMS id is readable on every record, but it cannot be set when creating a ticket.
Permission to enter and preferred access time are readable, but cannot be set through the API.
The published documentation shows no estimates.
The published documentation shows no invoices. The parts cost field is a parts total, not an invoice.
The published documentation shows no owner approval.
Create a ticket with POST /tickets.
Assign a technician or vendor by updating the ticket.
Set the status to Completed with a closing note. Companies that require a close-out photo cannot finish this way.
Set the status to Cancelled with a reason code.
Change the assigned technician or vendor on the ticket.

checklist.item: Approve or reject an estimate or invoice
checklist.note: The published documentation shows no way to approve or reject an estimate or invoice.

checks.title: Object coverage
checks.why: Objects earn 17.0 of 28 weighted points. Work orders, status changes, assignment, and units are fully covered; scheduling, estimates, invoices, and owner approval are absent, and six other objects are partial.

checks.title: Write coverage
checks.why: All three core workflows (create, assign, and complete a work order) work through the API, 9 of 9 weighted points. A company that requires a close-out photo has no way to complete through the API, because the published documentation shows no photo upload.

checks.title: Lifecycle coverage
checks.why: Cancelling a work order and reassigning the vendor or technician both work, 5 of 7 weighted points. The published documentation shows no way to approve or reject an estimate or invoice.

checks.title: Change notification
checks.why: 19 signed webhook events cover every critical change (create, status, assignment, cancel, and reassign), and updated_since works on every list except staff. Push covers 63.4% of the critical and important rows, with nothing for scheduling, photos, notes, PMS links, or entry permission.

checks.title: Modern API conventions
checks.why: Standard resource-based REST with GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE and JSON bodies, confirmed in live reads.

checks.title: Consistent typing
checks.why: Ids, true/false values, fixed lists, and timestamps are typed consistently, and live reads matched the schema. Two cost fields (ticket parts cost and utility reading cost) are plain decimal numbers rather than a precise money format; both are non-core.

checks.title: Structured errors
checks.why: Every error uses one shape with a stable code and a message, across 28 documented codes. Live tests returned the right code and status for missing records, bad requests, bad paging cursors, and bad keys.

checks.title: Duplicate prevention
checks.why: Every write requires an Idempotency-Key. A retried request returns the stored result instead of making a duplicate.

checks.title: Graceful handling under load
checks.why: The docs describe a limit of 120 calls a minute per key and a 429 reply with a Retry-After wait time. None of the 38 live responses carried a rate-limit header, so the documented behavior was not confirmed by an observed signal.

checks.title: Pagination for large collections
checks.why: Cursor paging in a stable id order, up to 200 rows a page, with a clear end signal. A live test walked a full list of 24 tickets with no overlaps.

checks.title: Bulk or incremental export
checks.why: Every object list except staff accepts updated_since, with written sync instructions, and live tests returned exactly the changed records. There is no dedicated bulk export job, but documented incremental sync meets this check.

checks.title: Webhook security and delivery reliability
checks.why: Webhooks are signed (HMAC-SHA256) with a five-minute replay window. Failed deliveries are retried at 1, 2, 4, 8, and 24 hours, and each event carries an id for de-duplication.

checks.title: Concurrency and conflict control
checks.why: Tickets, the only records the API edits in place, support ETag and If-Match; a stale write gets a 412 and nothing is saved. This is documented; testing was read-only, so it was not exercised.

checks.title: Versioning and backward compatibility
checks.why: The version is in the path (/api/v1), with a written list of breaking changes and dated deprecation notices. But notice is 90 days, below the required six months, one change shipped without that notice, and the terms let features change or be removed.

checks.title: Request traceability
checks.why: Every response carries an X-Request-Id you can quote to support. It appeared on all 38 live responses and echoed a value the tester sent.

checks.title: Service availability and status transparency
checks.why: A public status page shows 90-day uptime (100% for the app, developer docs, and website) and has an incident-history page. A written SLA exists only in Enterprise agreements, which this check does not require.

checks.title: Read-only credentials
checks.why: A read scope opens every list and fetch only. The key used for testing showed read scope with no write actions.

checks.title: Scoped credentials
checks.why: Three scopes (read, write, and webhook only), plus per-action limits on write keys, such as creating tickets only or recording occupancy only.

checks.title: Multiple keys
checks.why: Admins create and label a separate key for each integration. Rate limits count per key, so two integrations never use up each other's budget.

checks.title: Rotation and revocation
checks.why: Admins can revoke a key themselves at any time. A lost key is replaced by creating a new one and revoking the old one.

checks.title: Test environment and isolation
checks.why: The published documentation shows no API sandbox, test mode, or test key. The only test offering is a 7-day demo company with app logins, and it does not mention API access.

checks.title: Delegated access
checks.why: The published documentation shows no OAuth or other delegated sign-in into FixGrid; the docs call user-level OAuth a later step. The Procore connection signs in outward to Procore, not into FixGrid.

checks.title: Complete self-serve reference
checks.why: A public reference covers all 30 operations with auth, parameters, field tables, and a curl request example on each. No operation shows a sample response body; only two guide pages do.

checks.title: Reliable machine-consumable integration path
checks.why: A public OpenAPI 3.1 file, no key needed, covers all 30 operations and all 17 objects, and the API serves the same file. Three path parameters are not declared, a small fix. There is no SDK and no MCP server.

checks.title: AI-readable documentation
checks.why: Developer llms.txt and a single-file llms-full.txt hold every guide and the full reference in plain text. The site's robots.txt allows AI crawlers.

checks.title: Kept current
checks.why: A dated changelog has frequent entries from Sep 8 to Nov 9, 2026, each saying what changed and whether it adds or breaks. Minor slips: two changes were written up about 12 days late (both disclosed), and one entry's operation count is out of date.

checks.title: Self-serve API key
checks.why: A Company Admin creates keys inside FixGrid. The docs say you do not apply to FixGrid for a key, and there is no ticket or approval.

checks.title: Not commercially gated
checks.why: The public API and signed webhooks are included on every plan, Starter through Enterprise, with no partner fee and no API add-on. One rate limit applies to all keys.

runs.agreement: 26 of 28 checks unanimous; 19 of 20 checklist items unanimous

disagreements.why: FixGrid says it is maintenance-first, not a full PMS, and units come from the PMS by rent-roll file, so creating or editing the property roster is not this item's job. Units are readable with filters and change syncing, and occupancy writes exist.
disagreements.score_effect: none (at 0.5, coverage would be 68.18%, still a B and still 87)

disagreements.why: This difference follows directly from checklist item 7.

The OpenAPI file covers all 30 operations, schemas for all 17 objects, and request examples on every write. The flaw is three undeclared path parameters, a small fix rather than the substantial correction a partial requires.
disagreements.score_effect: none (at partial, the share would be 79.55%, still 87)

runs.summary: All three runs scored 87 (B+), with the same gates and no MCP step. The two disputes were settled against the frozen evidence, and every alternate reading, alone or together, still gives 87 (B+). C1.4 was partial in all three runs, though Run 2 counted webhook coverage at 68.3% instead of 63.4%.

strengths: API and signed webhooks included on every plan, with no extra fee
Admins create API keys themselves, with no sales call or approval
Create, assign, complete, cancel, and reopen work orders through the API
Read-only and per-action keys limit what each tool can do
Every write takes an idempotency key, so retries never create duplicates
Overwrite protection stops one edit silently replacing another on a ticket
Change syncing on every object list except staff
Signed, retried webhooks for new tickets, status changes, and assignments
Clear error codes and a support-ready request id on every response
Public OpenAPI spec and one-file AI-readable docs, no login needed
watch: The published documentation shows no appointment scheduling on work orders
The published documentation shows no photo upload, which blocks photo-required close-outs
Ticket notes can be added but cannot be read back through the API
The published documentation shows no way to add, edit, or deactivate vendors
The published documentation shows no resident records to read
The published documentation shows no estimates, invoices, or owner approvals
The published documentation shows no API sandbox, so testing uses a real account
No "sign in with FixGrid" option, so connecting a tool means sharing a key
Only 90 days' notice for breaking changes, and one change skipped it
No rate-limit headers on live responses, so you can't see the limit coming
bottom: FixGrid is a maintenance system that runs beside your PMS. It is not a PMS or a bank. Its API is free on every plan and well built: you can pull your maintenance data out and push in the core work-order actions (create, assign, complete, cancel, and reopen tickets), plus record notices and move-ins. Its biggest strength is careful engineering, with read-only and per-action keys, safe retries, overwrite protection, documented change syncing, signed webhooks, and AI-friendly docs. Its biggest limit is reach: the published documentation shows no way to schedule appointments, add photos, read notes, add or edit vendors, read residents, or handle estimates, invoices, or owner approvals, and there is no API sandbox or "sign in with FixGrid" option. You still need your PMS for leasing, residents, and accounting, and today the two share data by file, not live sync.
provider_fit: FixGrid is maintenance-management software (a CMMS) built for multifamily operators, not a PMS or a bank. You still need your PMS for leasing, residents, and accounting, and today data moves between them by rent-roll file and CSV, not live sync.
